To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
education in Africa has become a compendium of knowledge that is not African.

education in Africa has not been decolonised, and that this is due to the resilience of a colonial and colonizing educational epistemology that takes the form of a science as ideology and a science as hegemony.
The resilience of the colonial and colonizing education in Africa is a consequence of the hegemonic power and ideology of science and the epistemology it inspires.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which education in Africa is still being used to perpetuate colonial and colonizing ideology and hegemony, and the need for a critical and reflexive approach to the education of African children.
the question: What are the effects of education on African people and their societies?
the question of how to re-orientate the African educational system to be more relevant to the needs of the continent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the education system in Africa has not changed much since colonial times.
the paper is a call for a rethinking of the epistemology of education in Africa, which is a call to rethink the very idea of education in Africa.
education in Africa has been and is still being used as a tool for the perpetuation of colonialism and colonialism in Africa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper argues that education in Africa has become a tool for Africans to ‘become like’ the colonizer.
education in Africa needs to be re-imagined and reconstructed to be relevant, meaningful and liberating.
education in Africa has become a compunction to lighten the darkness, both physically and metaphorical, in order to be competitive in the interest of colonizing and dominating others.
The main takeaway from our work is that
African scholars and educators should not only be critical of the resilience of colonial and colonizing education, but also be critical of their own complicity with it.

the resilience of colonial education in Africa can only be overcome through the agency of ordinary people, who can be empowered to question, challenge and resist hegemonic and epistemological coloniality.
the resilience of the colonial epistemology in education is a result of the complicity of the elite, and a failure to listen to the voices and wisdom of ordinary men and women.
